examples.note: Mentioning the title without 'Anon' or 'Anonymous'.

parts.quote: Beowulf is the story of a hero who defeats a dragon.

examples.note: In-text citation omitting author placeholder.

parts.quote: Like Grendel (Beowulf), you seem to suffer with the joy of others.

examples.note: Uses 'Anon' in citation.

parts.quote: Beowulf (Anon) is the story of a hero who defeats a dragon.

examples.note: Uses 'Anonymous' in citation.

parts.quote: Like Grendel (Anonymous Beowulf), you seem to suffer with the joy of others.

rules.quote: If you don’t know the name of the author, don’t use ‘Anon’,‘unknown’ or ‘Anonymous’ in the in-text citation.
rules.violation_condition: an in-text citation for an author-unknown classic that includes 'Anon', 'unknown', or 'Anonymous'
when: The author of the classic work being cited is unknown.
rules.why: G-4: Specific prohibition on placeholder author names in in-text citations.

examples.note: Uses common name 'Cicero'.

parts.quote: As Cicero expressed it, ‘Is there anything rasher and more unworthy of the dignity and strength of character of a wise man than the holding of a false opinion?’ (On the nature of the gods)

examples.note: Uses full name 'Marcus Tullius Cicero' instead of common name.

parts.quote: As Marcus Tullius Cicero expressed it, ‘Is there anything rasher and more unworthy of the dignity and strength of character of a wise man than the holding of a false opinion?’ (On the nature of the gods)

rules.quote: Use the author’s common name in text, in-text citations and reference lists.
rules.violation_condition: using a classical author's full name (such as given name and surname) rather than their common name
when: Referring to authors of classical and medieval periods who are known by a common name.
rules.why: G-4: Heading restated directly by body instruction.

examples.note: Author Cicero is in the sentence; citation contains only the title.

parts.quote: As Cicero expressed it, ‘Is there anything rasher and more unworthy of the dignity and strength of character of a wise man than the holding of a false opinion?’ (On the nature of the gods)

rules.quote: As with other books, if you mention the author in the sentence, don’t place the author’s name in brackets with the title of the work.
rules.violation_condition: placing the author's name inside citation brackets when the author is already mentioned in the surrounding sentence
when: The author is mentioned in the sentence.
rules.why: G-2: Standard rule against repeating named author inside in-text citation brackets.

covers.quote: If the work you’re citing has divisions, quote them in the in-text citation.

examples.note: First citation spelling out divisions with commas.

parts.quote: (Ovid The art of love, book 3, line 810)

examples.note: First citation with divisions spelled out.

parts.quote: Josh hesitated at the doorway until, like Dante, he ‘went on, timid and full of thought.’ (Dante The divine comedy, canto 20, line 151)

rules.quote: The first time you cite a work, spell out the divisions. Place a comma between the title of the work and the first division. Separate divisions with a comma.
rules.violation_condition: in the first in-text citation of a classic work with divisions, failing to spell out divisions or failing to separate the title and divisions with commas
when: The citation is the first citation of a classic work with multiple divisions.
rules.why: G-2: Specific punctuation and formatting rule for initial division citations.

examples.note: Subsequent citation with division numbers separated by a full stop.

parts.quote: (Ovid The art of love3.815)

examples.note: Subsequent citation using division numbers separated by full stop.

parts.quote: (Dante The divine comedy 20.151)

rules.quote: For subsequent citations, don’t spell out the divisions. You only need the division numbers. Separate divisions with a full stop. Don’t place a comma between the title of the work and the division numbers.
rules.violation_condition: in subsequent in-text citations of a classic work with divisions, spelling out the divisions, including a comma after the title, or failing to separate division numbers with a full stop
when: The citation is a subsequent citation of a classic work with divisions.
rules.why: G-2: Specific formatting rule for subsequent citations of classics with divisions.

examples.note: Single division spelled out with a comma after the title.

parts.quote: Virgil and Dante argue over the value of pitying the sinners in their suffering. (Dante The divine comedy, canto 20)

rules.quote: If you have only one division to cite, always spell it out. Place a comma between the title and the division.
rules.violation_condition: abbreviating a single division or failing to place a comma between the title and the division
when: Citing only one division of a classic work.
rules.why: G-2: Exception/rule for single division citations.

covers.quote: If you’re referring to an edition that doesn’t have divisions, you can refer to specific page numbers.

examples.note: Date and page separated by an unspaced colon.

parts.quote: As one of the early philosophers wrote, ‘All wars are undertaken for the acquisition of wealth.’ (Plato Phaedo 1954:85)

examples.note: Citation without divisions using date:page format.

parts.quote: Josh hesitated at the doorway until, like Dante, he ‘went on, timid and full of thought.’ (The divine comedy 1954:265)

rules.quote: In these cases, place the date of the translation – or edition – you’re working with and the page number after the title of the work. Separate the date from the page numbers with a colon, not a full stop. Don’t use spaces around the colon.
rules.violation_condition: in a classic citation without divisions, using a separator other than an unspaced colon between date and page number, or separating with spaces around the colon
when: Referring to an edition of a classic work that does not have divisions.
rules.why: G-2: Rule governing citations when division numbers are absent.

covers.quote: In these cases, cite the title in the original language.

examples.note: Anglicised spelling.

parts.quote: Troiades

examples.note: Original Greek alphabet used.

parts.quote: Τρῳάδες

rules.quote: If the original language uses a different alphabet to English – ancient Greek for example – use the anglicised spelling.
rules.violation_condition: citing a title in a non-Latin script (such as ancient Greek characters) rather than an anglicised spelling
when: Citing a title in an original language that uses a non-Latin alphabet.
rules.why: G-2, G-4: Transliteration/anglicisation requirement for non-Latin titles.

covers.quote: Place the date at the end of the reference.
specify the date of the edition, not the date of the creation of the work

examples.note: Date '1954' placed at end of reference list entry.

parts.quote: Plato, Phaedo(Tredennick H, trans), Penguin, Harmondsworth, 1954.

examples.note: Date placed at the end.

parts.quote: Dante, The divine comedy (Ruse HR, trans), Holt, Rinehart and Winston, New York, 1954.

rules.quote: place the date at the end of the reference list entry – this is contrary to author–date style, but it stops possible confusion caused by, for example, ‘Plato (1954)’
rules.violation_condition: in a reference list entry for a classic work, placing the publication date immediately after the author instead of at the end of the entry
when: Including a classic work in an author-date reference list.
rules.why: G-2: Specific exception to standard author-date format for reference list entries of classics.
